warmup.q: A Spring bean has @Transactional public void settle(String id) and an unannotated settleAll(List<String> ids) that calls settle(id) in a loop. A REST resource calls settleAll with three ids. How many transactions does Spring start?
options: It depends on the isolation level
warmup.why: The transaction lives in the proxy, and the proxy only sees calls that come through it. The resource calls settleAll through the proxy, but settleAll has no annotation. The three settle calls go through this, straight to the real object, so the advice never runs. Quarkus intercepts self-invocation, so the same code there would start three.

sections.h: Decorator: same interface, one more behavior
sections.html:
new DataOutputStream(new BufferedOutputStream(new GZIPOutputStream(out))) is three decorators around one stream. Each wrapper is an OutputStream too. Each adds one behavior (typed writes, buffering, compression) and passes the bytes on to the stream it wraps. The JDK's FilterInputStream Javadoc describes it plainly: it "wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way".

That is the whole pattern. A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, does one extra thing, and forwards the call. Callers can't tell how many layers there are.

Fees fit it well, because a fee is a base rule plus adjustments. In Java, a functional interface with default methods turns each adjustment into a one-line decorator. Each method returns a new lambda that calls the calculator it wraps:

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface FeeCalculator {
    long feeMinor(Payment p);

    static FeeCalculator percent(int bps) { return p -> p.amountMinor() * bps / 10_000; }
    default FeeCalculator plusFixed(long fixed) { return p -> feeMinor(p) + fixed; }
    default FeeCalculator crossBorder(String home, int extraBps) {
        return p -> feeMinor(p) + (p.country().equals(home) ? 0 : p.amountMinor() * extraBps / 10_000);
    }
    default FeeCalculator cappedAt(long cap) { return p -> Math.min(feeMinor(p), cap); }
}

FeeCalculator standard = FeeCalculator.percent(290).plusFixed(30).crossBorder("DE", 100).cappedAt(500);
Kotlin
fun interface FeeCalculator {
    fun feeMinor(p: Payment): Long
}

fun percent(bps: Int) = FeeCalculator { p -> p.amountMinor * bps / 10_000 }
fun FeeCalculator.plusFixed(fixed: Long) = FeeCalculator { p -> feeMinor(p) + fixed }
fun FeeCalculator.crossBorder(home: String, extraBps: Int) =
    FeeCalculator { p -> feeMinor(p) + if (p.country == home) 0 else p.amountMinor * extraBps / 10_000 }
fun FeeCalculator.cappedAt(cap: Long) = FeeCalculator { p -> minOf(feeMinor(p), cap) }

val standard = percent(290).plusFixed(30).crossBorder("DE", 100).cappedAt(500)

In Kotlin the decorators are extension functions on a fun interface. Either way, every call returns a new calculator and leaves the one it wraps alone.

Order matters. With standard, a domestic 100.00 EUR payment costs 3.20, a French one costs 4.20, and a French 1,000.00 EUR payment hits the cap at 5.00. Move cappedAt(500) before crossBorder and that last payment costs 15.00, because the surcharge now lands after the cap. Both chains compile. Only a test with a large cross-border payment tells them apart.

Behavior decorators have the same issue. A retry decorator outside a logging decorator logs every attempt. Swap them and you log one call, however many attempts it took. Pick the order you want and pin it in a test.

try.title: Stack two decorators in both orders
steps: Open DecoratorStack.java (or DecoratorStack.kt). The issuer fails twice, then approves. Logging records each call it sees; Retrying tries up to three times.
Before you run it, write down how many log lines each of the two stacks produces.
Run it with the command below. Then decide: if Logging fed your request-rate metric, which order would you want?

code.title: DecoratorStack.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Two decorators around a flaky issuer. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. */ public class DecoratorStack { interface IssuerCall { String authorize(long amountMinor); } // the real client: fails twice, then succeeds static final class FlakyIssuer implements IssuerCall { private int calls; public String authorize(long amountMinor) { if (++calls <= 2) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer timeout #" + calls); return "A-" + amountMinor; } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it record Logging(IssuerCall inner, List<String> log) implements IssuerCall { public String authorize(long amountMinor) { log.add("authorize " + amountMinor); return inner.authorize(amountMinor); } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times record Retrying(IssuerCall inner, int attempts) implements IssuerCall { public String authorize(long amountMinor) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return inner.authorize(amountMinor); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw last; } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); IssuerCall retryOutside = new Retrying(new Logging(new FlakyIssuer(), log), 3); System.out.println("Retrying(Logging(issuer)): " + retryOutside.authorize(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); log.clear(); IssuerCall logOutside = new Logging(new Retrying(new FlakyIssuer(), 3), log); System.out.println("Logging(Retrying(issuer)): " + logOutside.authorize(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); } }

alt.title: DecoratorStack.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 // Two decorators around a flaky issuer. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. fun interface IssuerCall { fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String } // the real client: fails twice, then succeeds class FlakyIssuer : IssuerCall { private var calls = 0 override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { check(++calls > 2) { "issuer timeout #$calls" } return "A-$amountMinor" } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it class Logging(private val inner: IssuerCall, private val log: MutableList<String>) : IssuerCall { override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { log += "authorize $amountMinor" return inner.authorize(amountMinor) } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times class Retrying(private val inner: IssuerCall, private val attempts: Int) : IssuerCall { override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return inner.authorize(amountMinor) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e } } throw last!! } } fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() val retryOutside = Retrying(Logging(FlakyIssuer(), log), 3) println("Retrying(Logging(issuer)): ${retryOutside.authorize(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") log.clear() val logOutside = Logging(Retrying(FlakyIssuer(), 3), log) println("Logging(Retrying(issuer)): ${logOutside.authorize(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") }

try.expect: Retrying(Logging(issuer)): A-1250, log lines: 3 and Logging(Retrying(issuer)): A-1250, log lines: 1. The outer decorator sees one logical call; the inner one sees every attempt. For a request-rate metric you want logging outside (one per request). For an issuer error-rate metric you want it inside, where the two failures are visible.

video.title: A decorator wraps the same interface: the call goes in layer by layer, and the order of the layers changes the fee

sections.h: Kotlin's by writes the forwarding for you
sections.html:
A hand-written decorator for Map in Java must forward every method (get, put, remove, size, entrySet and many more) just to change one. Kotlin's class delegation writes the forwarding for you:

Java
// Java has no `by`. The short way is inheritance, and HashMap's internals decide what you count.
class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> {
    int puts;
    @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); }
}
Kotlin
class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner {
    var puts = 0
    override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++; return inner.put(key, value) }
}

: MutableMap<K, V> by inner tells the compiler to generate every method of the interface as a call on inner, except the ones you override. The Kotlin docs call delegation "a good alternative to implementation inheritance".

Now predict. After put("a", 1) and putAll(mapOf("b" to 2, "c" to 3)), what is puts? It is 1, and size is 3. The compiler forwards putAll to inner.putAll, and inner is a plain HashMap that has never heard of your override. The docs say so: overridden members "do not get called from the members of the delegate object". To count every insertion, override putAll too, and putIfAbsent, compute and merge.

That surprise is also the benefit. With inheritance, the answer depends on how the parent class is written today. HashMap.putAll happens not to call put, so the Java count is also 1. HashSet.addAll does call add, so a set that counts in both methods counts each element twice. Effective Java item 18 is built on that bug. With by, the delegate never calls back into your code, so a JDK update can't change your count.

The JDK has a read-only decorator you use often: Collections.unmodifiableList. It forwards reads and throws UnsupportedOperationException on writes. It is a view. Its Javadoc says queries "read through" to the list it wraps, so later changes to that list show up in the view. For a snapshot, use List.copyOf. Kotlin's List type is weaker still: a read-only interface on the same object, with no wrapper at all.

Java
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing);
backing.add("capture");        // view now shows it too
view.add("refund");            // UnsupportedOperationException
Kotlin
val view: List<String> = backing          // same object, read-only type
backing += "capture"                       // view now shows it too
(view as MutableList).add("refund")        // works: nothing guards it

try.title: Count what the delegate does behind your back
steps: Read CountingMapDemo.kt. Predict puts after one put and a putAll of two entries, and added after addAll of three elements.
Run it with the command below.
Now run the Java twin, CountingMapDemoJava, which uses extends HashMap and extends HashSet with the same overrides. Predict first: will the Java numbers match?

code.title: CountingMapDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 // Decorators built with `by`: the compiler writes every forwarding method for you. class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 private set override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++ return inner.put(key, value) } } class CountingSet<E>(private val inner: MutableSet<E> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<E> by inner { var added = 0 private set override fun add(element: E): Boolean { added++ return inner.add(element) } override fun addAll(elements: Collection<E>): Boolean { added += elements.size return inner.addAll(elements) // inner's addAll calls inner's add, never ours } } fun main() { val m = CountingMap<String, Int>() m["a"] = 1 // goes through our put m.putAll(mapOf("b" to 2, "c" to 3)) // forwarded to inner.putAll, which never calls our put println("CountingMap: puts=${m.puts}, size=${m.size}") val s = CountingSet<String>() s.addAll(listOf("x", "y", "z")) println("CountingSet: added=${s.added}, size=${s.size}") }

alt.title: CountingMapDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.Collection; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * The Java twin of CountingMapDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so the short way is inheritance, * and then the result depends on how the parent class happens to be written. */ public class CountingMapDemoJava { static final class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } // Effective Java item 18: HashSet.addAll calls add for each element, so this counts twice static final class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> { int added; @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); } @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { CountingMap<String, Integer> m = new CountingMap<>(); m.put("a", 1); m.putAll(Map.of("b", 2, "c", 3)); // HashMap.putAll doesn't call put, today System.out.println("CountingMap: puts=" + m.puts + ", size=" + m.size()); CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>(); s.addAll(List.of("x", "y", "z")); System.out.println("CountingSet: added=" + s.added + ", size=" + s.size()); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints puts=1, size=3 and added=3, size=3: the delegate never calls your overrides, so you count exactly what you wrote. Java prints puts=1, size=3 but added=6, size=3, because HashSet.addAll calls add for each element and the override counts them a second time. With inheritance, your count depends on the parent's internals.

sections.h: Dynamic proxies: one handler for every method
sections.html:
A decorator is written for one interface. A dynamic proxy is written once and works for any interface. java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates a class at runtime that implements the interfaces you name, and sends every call to one InvocationHandler:

Java
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) {
    InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> {
        Throwable last = null;
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            try {
                return method.invoke(target, args);
            } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                last = e.getCause();             // unwrap: the target's own exception
            }
        }
        throw last;
    };
    return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler);
}
Kotlin
inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T =
    Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args ->
        var last: Throwable? = null
        repeat(maxAttempts) {
            try {
                return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray()))
            } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) {
                last = e.cause                    // unwrap: the target's own exception
            }
        }
        throw last!!
    } as T

The handler gets the proxy, the Method being called and its arguments. It can run code before and after, and it decides whether to call the real object at all. A retry, a timer or an authorization check is written once and covers every method of every client.

Two rules catch everyone the first time. First, method.invoke wraps whatever the target throws in an InvocationTargetException. Unwrap it with getCause() and rethrow that. If the wrapper escapes, the proxy sees a checked exception that charge never declared, and the caller gets an UndeclaredThrowableException wrapping an InvocationTargetException wrapping the real error. No catch (IllegalStateException e) in the caller will match it.

Second, JDK proxies implement interfaces only. They can't extend a class. For classes, frameworks generate a subclass at runtime (Spring uses CGLIB), and a subclass can't override final methods.

The Kotlin version is shorter for one reason: reified T lets the function read T::class.java itself, so callers write retrying(flaky, 3) and pass no Class object.

Before you wrap a PSP client in this, know that it retries everything, charge included. If the first attempt timed out after the PSP took the money, the second attempt charges the card again. Retry only idempotent operations, or send an idempotency key the PSP deduplicates on. The worked example does exactly that.

try.title: Break the retry proxy two ways
steps: Run RetryingProxyDemo (Java or Kotlin) and read the first two lines.
In main, change retrying(PspClient.class, flaky, 3) to 2 attempts (retrying(flaky, 2) in Kotlin). Predict what the caller sees, then run.
Keep 2 attempts. In the handler, replace last = e.getCause() with last = e (in Kotlin, last = e.cause becomes last = e). Predict the exception type, then run. Undo both changes.

code.title: RetryingProxyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. */ public class RetryingProxyDemo { interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); } interface Ledger { void post(String entry); void postTwice(String entry); } static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.getCause(); } } throw last; }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> trace) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { trace.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] calls = {0}; PspClient flaky = (token, amount) -> { if (++calls[0] < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("PSP 503"); return "ch_" + amount; }; PspClient psp = retrying(PspClient.class, flaky, 3); System.out.println("charge -> " + psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250) + " after " + calls[0] + " target calls"); System.out.println("proxy class: " + Proxy.isProxyClass(psp.getClass())); List<String> trace = new ArrayList<>(); Ledger real = new Ledger() { public void post(String entry) { } public void postTwice(String entry) { post(entry); post(entry); } // this.post(): skips the proxy }; tracing(Ledger.class, real, trace).postTwice("fee 3.20"); System.out.println("calls the proxy saw: " + trace); } }

alt.title: RetryingProxyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. fun interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String } interface Ledger { fun post(entry: String); fun postTwice(entry: String) } // reified T replaces the Class<T> parameter the Java version needs inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> var last: Throwable? = null repeat(maxAttempts) { try { return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.cause } } throw last!! } as T inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, trace: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> trace += method.name try { method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } as T fun main() { var calls = 0 val flaky = PspClient { _, amount -> check(++calls >= 3) { "PSP 503" } "ch_$amount" } val psp = retrying(flaky, 3) println("charge -> ${psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250)} after $calls target calls") println("proxy class: ${Proxy.isProxyClass(psp.javaClass)}") val trace = mutableListOf<String>() val real = object : Ledger { override fun post(entry: String) {} override fun postTwice(entry: String) { post(entry); post(entry) } // this.post(): skips the proxy } tracing<Ledger>(real, trace).postTwice("fee 3.20") println("calls the proxy saw: $trace") }

try.expect: The first run prints charge -> ch_1250 after 3 target calls and proxy class: true. With 2 attempts the program dies with IllegalStateException: PSP 503, the target's own exception. Without the unwrap it dies with java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException, caused by an InvocationTargetException, caused by the IllegalStateException: a checked wrapper escaped a method that doesn't declare it.

sections.h: Framework proxies and the self-invocation trap
sections.html:
Spring and Quarkus make your annotations work with proxies. When a bean has @Transactional, @Retryable or @Cacheable, the container doesn't hand out your object. It hands out a proxy that begins the transaction (or retries, or checks the cache) and then calls your object. Spring uses a JDK dynamic proxy when the bean implements an interface and a CGLIB subclass when it doesn't. Spring Boot may switch to class-based proxies by default, depending on its configuration.

The proxy only sees calls that come through it. Look at this service:

Java
@Service
class SettlementService {
    public void settleAll(List<String> batchIds) {
        for (String id : batchIds) settle(id);       // really this.settle(id)
    }

    @Transactional
    public void settle(String batchId) { /* post to the ledger */ }
}
Kotlin
@Service
class SettlementService {
    fun settleAll(batchIds: List<String>) {
        for (id in batchIds) settle(id)              // really this.settle(id)
    }

    @Transactional
    fun settle(batchId: String) { /* post to the ledger */ }
}

A REST resource calls settleAll on the proxy. settleAll has no annotation, so the proxy just forwards it. Inside, settle(id) is a plain call on the target object. The proxy never sees it, so no transaction starts. Spring's docs put it this way: "self invocation via an explicit or implicit this reference will bypass the advice." The same goes for private and final methods, which a proxy can't override.

Spring's docs rank the fixes. Best: restructure so the call crosses a bean boundary (move settle to its own bean). Next: inject the bean into itself and call through that reference. Last: AopContext.currentProxy(), which they call "highly discouraged".

Quarkus behaves differently. Its CDI container, ArC, supports "intercepted self-invocation", so the same code in a Quarkus service does start a transaction for each settle call. The Quarkus docs flag this as non-standard, because the CDI specification doesn't say whether self-interception should work. Code that moves between the two frameworks can change behavior without a single edited line.

Kotlin adds one more trap. Classes and members are final unless marked open, and a CGLIB subclass can't override what is final. The kotlin-spring compiler plugin (a preset of all-open) opens classes that carry Spring annotations, so add it to every Kotlin Spring project. Quarkus transforms final classes for you, because quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default.

Check yourself. In the Spring SettlementService, you move @Transactional from settle to settleAll and change nothing else. How many transactions does the REST call start now, and how many batches does each one cover? (One, covering all three batches. The outside call to settleAll goes through the proxy, so it starts a transaction. The inner settle calls still skip the proxy, so they run as plain method calls inside that one transaction.)

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 262" role="img" aria-label="A caller's call goes through the proxy into settleAll on the real bean; the inner call this.settle() goes straight to settle and never passes the proxy"><rect class="box" x="16" y="100" width="110" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="71" y="121" text-anchor="middle">caller</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="71" y="139" text-anchor="middle">REST resource</text><rect class="box-a" x="170" y="78" width="180" height="92" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="260" y="104" text-anchor="middle">proxy</text><text class="t-s" x="260" y="126" text-anchor="middle">begin tx, retry, time</text><text class="t-s" x="260" y="146" text-anchor="middle">then forward the call</text><rect class="box-dim" x="400" y="16" width="270" height="214" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="535" y="36" text-anchor="middle">the real bean (target)</text><rect class="box" x="440" y="56" width="190" height="44" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="535" y="83" text-anchor="middle">settleAll()</text><rect class="box" x="440" y="164" width="190" height="52" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="535" y="184" text-anchor="middle">@Transactional</text><text class="t t-code" x="535" y="205" text-anchor="middle">settle(id)</text><line class="ln-a" x1="126" y1="124" x2="166" y2="124" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="350" y1="110" x2="436" y2="82" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="160" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-bad" x="598" y="135" text-anchor="middle">this.settle()</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="340" y="252" text-anchor="middle">the inner call never passes the proxy: no transaction</text></svg>
figure.caption: Calls from outside go through the proxy. A call through this inside the bean goes straight to the target, so the transaction never starts.

analogy: A decorator is a set of sleeves on a parcel: bubble wrap, then a box, then a shipping label. Each layer adds one thing, and the courier still handles it as one parcel. A proxy is the front desk of an office building: every visitor from outside signs in, gets checked and is sent up. The analogy holds for self-invocation, too: when someone already inside walks to the next office, they never pass the front desk. It breaks on judgment. A receptionist notices that the same visitor came in three times today; a proxy sees only one method name and its arguments, so it retries a charge as happily as a read unless you tell it which is which.
world: Your Quarkus services run on proxies already: @Transactional, and the MicroProfile Fault Tolerance annotations such as @Retry and @Timeout, work through interceptors that ArC wires around your beans. Because ArC intercepts self-invocation, a Quarkus @Transactional method called from the same bean does run in a transaction, so a Spring habit of moving it to another bean is harmless there but a Quarkus habit of calling it directly breaks when the code moves to Spring. Temporal's Java SDK hands you activity stubs that are proxies of your activity interface: the call you write becomes a scheduled activity task. And a metrics or tracing wrapper around a Kafka producer, or around the card-issuer client that takes 120 ms, is a decorator: put it inside the retry if you want to see every attempt.
mistake: The most common mistake is putting @Transactional (or @Retryable, or @Cacheable) on a Spring method that is only ever called from another method of the same bean. The code compiles, the tests with a mocked repository pass, and in production the inner call runs with no transaction, because this.settle() skips the proxy. People make it because the annotation sits right there on the method and looks like part of it, when it really lives in the proxy. The fix is to move the annotated method to its own bean, so the call crosses a proxy, or to put the annotation on the method the outside world calls. For Kotlin beans, also check that the kotlin-spring plugin is applied, or the proxy can't override the method at all.

compare.title: A timing decorator for a three-method port

java.title: TimedGateway.java
java.html: interface PaymentGateway { String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor); void capture(String authId); void refund(String authId, long amountMinor); } // one method changes; the other two are forwarded by hand final class TimedGateway implements PaymentGateway { private final PaymentGateway inner; private final Map<String, Long> nanos; TimedGateway(PaymentGateway inner, Map<String, Long> nanos) { this.inner = inner; this.nanos = nanos; } @Override public String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return inner.authorize(pan, amountMinor); } finally { nanos.merge("authorize", System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } @Override public void capture(String authId) { inner.capture(authId); } @Override public void refund(String authId, long amountMinor) { inner.refund(authId, amountMinor); } }

kotlin.title: TimedGateway.kt
kotlin.html: interface PaymentGateway { fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String fun capture(authId: String) fun refund(authId: String, amountMinor: Long) } // `by inner` generates capture and refund; you write only what changes class TimedGateway( private val inner: PaymentGateway, private val nanos: MutableMap<String, Long>, ) : PaymentGateway by inner { override fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return inner.authorize(pan, amountMinor) } finally { nanos.merge("authorize", System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } }

compare.note: The behavior is identical. What differs is who writes the forwarding: Java makes you type capture and refund, and Kotlin's by inner generates them. That has a second effect when the port grows. Add void voidAuth(String authId) to the interface and the Java decorator stops compiling until someone decides what it should do with the new method. The Kotlin one forwards it silently, untimed. Neither is wrong, but know which one you have. And remember that by has no open recursion: if the real gateway's capture calls its own authorize, that inner call is not timed. Kotlin makes the hand-written forwarding class unnecessary; it doesn't make Decorator unnecessary.

worked.title: Make a retry proxy safe for payments

steps.say: A teammate wrapped the PSP client in the generic retrying proxy from this lesson, with three attempts. The PSP sometimes answers a charge after 2 seconds, and the HTTP client gives up at 1.5 seconds. Before reading on, say what the customer sees on a slow day.
steps.code: interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); String status(String chargeId); } PspClient psp = retrying(PspClient.class, new HttpPspClient(), 3); psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250); // attempt 1 times out after the PSP has charged the card

alt.html: interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String fun status(chargeId: String): String } val psp = retrying<PspClient>(HttpPspClient(), 3) psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250) // attempt 1 times out after the PSP has charged the card

steps.say: Attempt one timed out on our side, but the PSP finished it. Attempts two and three are new charges, so the customer pays two or three times. Retrying is only safe for idempotent operations. Make that visible in the interface: mark the methods that may be repeated.
steps.code: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark at runtime, so the handler can read it @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface Idempotent {} interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); // not marked: one attempt only @Idempotent String status(String chargeId); // a read: safe to repeat }

alt.html: @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark at runtime, so the handler can read it annotation class Idempotent interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String // not marked: one attempt only @Idempotent fun status(chargeId: String): String // a read: safe to repeat }

steps.say: The handler reads the mark before its loop. Unmarked methods get exactly one attempt. Why does method.isAnnotationPresent work here even though the annotation is on the interface, not on HttpPspClient? Because the Method the proxy receives is the interface's method.
steps.code: InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { int attempts = method.isAnnotationPresent(Idempotent.class) ? maxAttempts : 1; // 2. ask the method Throwable last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // 3. unwrap } } throw last; };

alt.html: val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, args -> val attempts = if (method.isAnnotationPresent(Idempotent::class.java)) maxAttempts else 1 // 2. ask the method var last: Throwable? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return@InvocationHandler method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // 3. unwrap } } throw last!! }

steps.say: Now make the charge itself safe to repeat. Most PSPs accept an idempotency key: a second request with the same key returns the first result instead of charging again. The key must come from the caller and stay the same on every attempt, so derive it from the order. A key generated inside the retry loop would be new on each attempt and protect nothing.
steps.code: interface PspClient { @Idempotent String charge(String idempotencyKey, String token, long amountMinor); // 4. the PSP deduplicates @Idempotent String status(String chargeId); } psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250); // 5. same key on every attempt

alt.html: interface PspClient { @Idempotent fun charge(idempotencyKey: String, token: String, amountMinor: Long): String // 4. the PSP deduplicates @Idempotent fun status(chargeId: String): String } psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250) // 5. same key on every attempt

lab.title: A fee decorator chain and a timing proxy
steps: Run the tests once. All twelve fail with UnsupportedOperationException.

In FeeCalculator, write percent as a lambda: p -> p.amountMinor() * bps / 10_000. Then write each default method so it returns a new lambda that calls feeMinor(p) (the calculator being decorated) and adds one rule.

In TimingProxy.wrap, build an InvocationHandler and pass it to Proxy.newProxyInstance. Forward methods declared by Object without timing. For the rest, read the clock, call method.invoke(target, args), read the clock again and report Interface.method.
Catch InvocationTargetException, report the call as failed, and rethrow e.getCause().
Run the tests until all twelve pass. Then read the self-invocation test and explain to yourself why only authorizeTwice is reported.
hints: Inside a default method, a bare feeMinor(p) means this.feeMinor(p), where this is the calculator you are decorating. The lambda you return captures it.
method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class is true for toString, equals and hashCode on a JDK proxy.
Report with iface.getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName(). throw e.getCause(); compiles because InvocationHandler.invoke is declared throws Throwable.

drill.title: A logging proxy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write static <T> T logging(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) (in Kotlin, inline fun <reified T : Any> logging(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T). It returns a JDK dynamic proxy that adds each method name to log, forwards the call, and lets the target's own exception reach the caller unwrapped. Then compare. Did you remember the unwrap?

answer.html: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T logging(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { log.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // the target's own exception, unwrapped } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: inline fun <reified T : Any> logging(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> log += method.name try { method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // the target's own exception, unwrapped } } as T

recap: A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior and forwards the rest. java.io streams and Collections.unmodifiableList are decorators.
Decorator order changes results: capping before a cross-border surcharge turns a 5.00 fee into 15.00, and retry outside logging logs every attempt.
Kotlin by generates the forwarding methods, but the delegate never calls your overrides: putAll skips your put.
A dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) sends every interface call to one handler. Unwrap InvocationTargetException, or callers get UndeclaredThrowableException.
Spring's proxies don't see this.method() calls, so @Transactional on a self-invoked method does nothing. Quarkus ArC intercepts self-invocation.
Kotlin classes are final by default: use the kotlin-spring plugin so Spring's subclass proxies can override them.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "I put @Transactional on settle() and it's ignored when settleAll() calls it. Spring is broken." Explain what is happening, give the fix you'd use, and say what would happen to the same code in Quarkus.
explain.answer: The transaction isn't part of the method. It lives in a proxy that Spring puts in front of the bean, and the proxy only runs its advice for calls that pass through it. The REST resource calls settleAll through the proxy, but settleAll isn't annotated, and its call to settle is this.settle(), a plain call on the real object that never touches the proxy. The cleanest fix is to move settle into its own bean and inject it, so each call crosses a proxy. Self-injection works too; AopContext.currentProxy() is discouraged. Quarkus ArC supports intercepted self-invocation as a non-standard feature, so there the same code would start a transaction for each settle call.

deeper.html:
Resilience4j is a decorator library by design. Its README says it provides "higher-order functions (decorators)" for any functional interface, lambda or method reference, and that you can stack more than one. Supplier<String> guarded = CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(breaker, psp::charge) returns a new supplier that wraps the old one, and you can wrap that again with Retry.decorateSupplier. The order question from this lesson comes back: a retry outside the breaker retries rejected calls, and a retry inside it counts every attempt as a breaker call. The last lesson of this track builds a breaker by hand.

Spring Framework 7.0 brought retry and concurrency limits into the core framework as annotations: @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. Both apply to "proxy-invoked methods", so self-invocation bypasses them exactly like @Transactional. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, which means four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Spring 7 also added @Proxyable(INTERFACES) and @Proxyable(TARGET_CLASS) to choose the proxy type for a single bean.

JDK proxy classes are final, extend java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and can be detected with Proxy.isProxyClass. Their names are unspecified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for them, which is why stack traces show $Proxy42.charge. A proxy also intercepts equals, hashCode and toString, so a proxy and its target are different objects to a HashSet unless the handler forwards those methods.

Decorator and Proxy have the same structure. The difference is intent: a decorator adds behavior the caller asked for (compression, a surcharge), and a proxy controls access to the real object (a transaction, an authorization check, a lazily created connection). Collections.unmodifiableList sits on the line, which is a good sign that the names are for talking about designs, not for sorting classes into boxes.
